newsitem.title: UK: Copper Market heading for December showdown.
newsitem.headline: Copper Market heading for December showdown.

text.p: The volatile London Metal Exchange (LME) copper market could be heading for a showdown next month, as physical tightness and the residue of the Sumitomo Corp affair bring matters to a head, traders said.
Since October, LME copper prices, spreads, and warehouse stocks have combined to create the volatility and uncertainty that was commonplace in the market throughout the 1990s.
"It may be getting towards an end-game...there are only a couple of months left to play out," analyst Ted Arnold of brokers Merrill Lynch said.

December, in particular key dates between December 16/18, may be critical, as big short positions in this month and a lack of physical metal combined to push the overall backwardation for cash/threes out to $247 on Tuesday.

Prices, meanwhile, hit $2,285 a tonne - the highest since the June 1996 shake-out when Sumitomo of Japan fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.
Inventory levels have shrunk dramatically, and are currently at 6-1/4 year lows of just 90,050 tonnes, against 275,775 tonnes in September when cash/threes was at a small contango.
The pressure on prices has finally broken the market out of a range which had ranged from just under $1,900 and just above $2,000 reflecting an impasse between major players with deep pockets.

Big speculative shorts had been defending the upside from large financial institutions who lifted stock off the LME to ensure downside options, the Sumitomo residue, would not be declared, traders said.
But the price advances of the last few weeks have resulted in many upside option positions that had seemed destined to be abandoned now likely to be exercised.
"A few weeks ago, it was the downside puts that everybody was worried about. Now its the upside calls, and there is some phenomenal open interest out there," a senior trader said.

The LME's December date currently stands just above $2,400, with December options being declared next week. If December stays above $2,400 then nearly 8,000 lots of puts, equivalent to some 200,000 tonnes of copper, will be abandoned.
But on the upside there are 2,165, 2,570, and 6,970 lots of $2,400, $2,500, and $2,600 calls open. There are also said to be substantial OTC positions.
"The way the market and the backwardation is going, you cannot rule out the possibility that some of those will be hit," the trader said.
As well as the options, there are substantial futures short positions concentrated around the December delivery date. December 16/18 was over $30 backwardation on Tuesday.
This period has become critical because of rolling forward of short positions from three, six and even 12 months ago, as well as end-year business, they said.
And because there is a genuine shortage of metal the backwardation is justified. Grade A cathodes, Russian off-grades, and scrap have been in short supply for some time.
High prices and backwardations should draw some metal out of the woodwork, and physical traders said there were more offers of scrap now in Europe.
Merrill's Arnold noted that scrap producers would undoubtedly take advantange of current high prices which are unlikely to prevail as 1997 progresses.
However, the overall fundamental tightness has not been alleviated. and some merchants even said there was a case for the LME to re-consider its limit on the daily backwardation.
This is currently one percent of the settlement price and was imposed earlier this year when stocks were some 300,000 tonnes.
At current stock levels there should be no limit, as anybody unable to deliver copper on the LME, usually a speculative short, can just pay a $23 a tonne penalty, they said.
Longs, many of them who have end-user requirements, will be compensated by that sum. But.."you cannot put that ($23/tonne) in a furnace," one said.
